Week one. Amandeep took his son Jatin's phone at nine every night and banned the Friday football group outright. Jatin said nothing, just shut his door hard. Three days later Amandeep found a second phone, an old one, charging behind the books.
Week two. Amandeep sat on Jatin's bed instead of shouting. "I was scared about the late walks home. That's the real reason." Jatin stared at the floor, then muttered, "You could've just said that."
Week four. They had worked it out together: football on Fridays, home by eight, phone out of the room at ten, and Jatin picks which weekend night runs late. On Friday a text arrived, unasked: "Leaving now 👍" Amandeep read it twice and smiled.

qa.q: What did Amandeep find charging behind the books?
qa.a: Amandeep found a second phone, an old one, charging behind the books.

qa.q: What was Jatin feeling when he shut his door hard in week one?
qa.a: He felt controlled and angry at a ban with no reason given, and the hidden phone shows he wanted to keep some freedom, even in secret.

qa.q: Which change in Amandeep's approach made the difference?
qa.a: He shared his real fear, then worked out limits together with Jatin and let him choose within them, which rebuilt trust.

qa.q: How does Amandeep feel when Jatin texts "Leaving now" without being asked?
qa.a: Relieved and touched 😊; the secrecy has turned into Jatin keeping him in the loop by choice.

grounding: It shows a father seeing strict rules produce secrecy and then shifting to explaining reasons, offering choices within limits and staying connected.

passage:
Shreya, you think your papa was always this calm? When he was fifteen, your Thatha ran this house like a police station. No friends after school, no cinema, radio off at eight. And your papa, such a sweet boy, started lying. He'd say he was at tuition and be at the cricket ground. Once he came home with a split lip and wouldn't say how.
Your Thatha was furious at first. Then one night I heard him on the verandah, talking to your papa quietly. "I made these rules because I'm afraid for you. Tell me which ones feel unfair." They sat there till midnight. After that it was cricket three evenings a week, home before dark, and Thatha even went to watch some matches.
The lies stopped. Not all at once, but they stopped.

qa.q: Where was Shreya's papa when he said he was at tuition?
qa.a: He was at the cricket ground.

qa.q: Why do you think Shreya's papa started lying at fifteen?
qa.a: The rules were so tight, with no friends, no cinema and the radio off at eight, that he felt he had no room of his own; hiding seemed the only way to get some freedom.

qa.q: What did Thatha do that helped end the lies?
qa.a: He explained his fear honestly, asked which rules felt unfair, and agreed on limits together, even going to watch some matches to stay close.

qa.q: How might Shreya see papa differently after hearing this story?
qa.a: Shreya might realise papa knows from experience how harsh rules push teenagers into secrets, which may explain the calm way he parents now.

grounding: It shows, through an elder's memory, a father who saw strict rules breed secrecy and changed to explaining reasons, giving choices within limits and staying close.

passage:
Sahil worked night shifts at a call centre, so his rules for Keerthana came by text: no going out, no phone after ten, no friends over. For a month she agreed to everything. Then her class teacher called to say Keerthana had missed two afternoons of school.
He wanted to take her phone away for a year. Instead, on his one free morning, with the water tanker blaring outside and an hour left before he had to sleep, he sat across from her with two cups of tea. "I made all those rules because I'm never here to see you. That's my worry, not your fault. Where were you?"
She had been at a friend's house, practising for a dance competition he'd said no to. They settled it before the tanker left: practice twice a week at the friend's house, with a call when she arrives.

qa.q: Why had Keerthana missed two afternoons of school?
qa.a: She had been at a friend's house, practising for a dance competition.

qa.q: What does Sahil's first urge to take her phone for a year suggest he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he felt angry and deceived after the teacher's call and wanted even stricter control.

qa.q: What did Sahil do in that short hour that worked?
qa.a: He admitted the rules came from his own worry, asked instead of accusing, and agreed on practice twice a week with a call on arrival, a choice within clear limits.

qa.q: What is it like for Keerthana when her father sits down with tea instead of shouting?
qa.a: She likely feels safe enough to tell the truth about the dance practice, because he takes the blame for his worry instead of making her the problem.

grounding: It shows a father noticing his strict rules led to secrecy and moving to reasons, choices within limits and connection despite little time.

passage:
In their Lajpat Nagar flat, Harish had a rule for every hour of fifteen-year-old Parul's day: home by six, no friends' houses, phone on the dining table after nine. By March he noticed things. Her messages were always deleted. She said she'd been at the library when a neighbour had seen her at the park. Once she slammed her door and didn't speak to him for two days.
One night Harish sat on the step outside her room. "I've been making rules without telling you why. Here's why: the main road is dark after seven, and I get scared. Can we choose together? Park with friends till seven, and you text me when you leave."
Parul opened the door a crack. "And the phone?"
"Your call, after ten."
The next evening she texted him from the park gate at five to seven: "Coming home. Want samosas?"

qa.q: What did a neighbour see that didn't match Parul's story?
qa.a: A neighbour had seen her at the park when she said she'd been at the library.

qa.q: How did Harish feel about Parul's secrecy, and what shows it?
qa.a: Harish felt scared for Parul and wanted to reconnect, which is why he sat on the step outside her room and admitted the dark main road frightens him.

qa.q: Which change in Harish's approach turned things around, and why?
qa.a: He explained the real reason for his worry and offered choices within limits, so Parul had room to decide and no need to hide.

qa.q: How might Parul have experienced her father's rules before that night?
qa.a: They probably felt like a cage with no reasons, so hiding and lying seemed the only way to have any life of her own.

grounding: A father sees his strict rules breed secrecy and defiance, then explains his reasons, offers choices within limits and reconnects.

"Kishore, sit. I'm not going to shout."
"That's new."
"Fair." Ujjwal pulled a chair close. "Last month I banned your late cricket evenings on the ground. Since then you've lied twice about where you were. Your mother found your kit in Faisal's car."
"Because you never listen, Papa. You just say no."
"You're right. I said no without reasons. Here's the reason: the ground has no lights and the road back is a highway. I lie awake."
Kishore looked up.
"So, choices. Weekend games, any time till dark. Or weekday games if someone's parent drives both ways. You pick."
"...Weekends. And Faisal's dad can drive sometimes."
"Deal. And tell me the score after. I actually want to know."
"You hate cricket."
"I like you."

qa.a: In Faisal's car.

qa.a: He let Kishore pick between weekend games till dark or weekday games with a parent driving, which kept the safety limit while giving Kishore a real say.

qa.q: How had the ban felt from Kishore's side?
qa.a: To Kishore it felt like being refused without being heard, so lying seemed easier than talking.

passage: Last year I was the strictest father in our building, and I was proud of it. I'm Darshan. My son Jeevan, fourteen, had a list of rules: phone off at nine, no going out after dark, no gaming at friends' houses. The more rules I added, the quieter he got. Then I found out he'd been going to a friend's place on Saturdays and telling me it was the library. That hurt more than I can say. I wanted to add a new rule. Instead, one night I sat on his bed and said, "Tell me which rule feels the most unfair, and I'll tell you why I made it." He was stunned. We talked for an hour. We kept the phone rule but moved it to ten. Saturdays at friends' are allowed now, if he messages me when he arrives. He hasn't lied since.

qa.q: Where did Jeevan say he was going on Saturdays?
qa.a: He said he was going to the library.

qa.q: What did Darshan feel on finding out about the Saturdays, and what did he choose to do?
qa.a: Darshan felt deeply hurt and tempted to add another rule, but chose to sit with Jeevan and talk about which rule felt unfair and why each existed.

qa.q: Which changes kept Jeevan safe while giving him some say?
qa.a: Keeping the phone rule but moving it to ten, and allowing Saturdays at friends' if he messages on arrival: limits with reasons and choices.

qa.q: How might Jeevan have felt when his father asked which rule felt most unfair?
qa.a: Jeevan was probably stunned and then relieved to be asked, which opened an hour of real talk.

grounding: Shows a father noticing that strict rules bred secrecy and switching to reasons, choices within limits and connection.

passage:
Parent journal, Sunday. Jomon.
Something shifted this week with Dhruv. For months I've been saying no to the late cycling rides with his friends. Every no made him slam doors, and on Friday I found out he had gone anyway, phone switched off. I was furious. Then I saw his face while I shouted: not guilt, just hardness. That scared me more than the ride. So yesterday I tried something else. I told him the real reason: the highway stretch with no lights, and the boy from Block C who was hit last year. Then I offered choices: rides until seven on any day, or later on weekends with lights on the bikes and his location shared. He picked weekends. He even asked me to check the lights. Tonight he texted from the ride: "Reached the lake. Lights on."

qa.q: What did Dhruv text from the ride?
qa.a: 'Reached the lake. Lights on.'

qa.q: What did Jomon feel on seeing Dhruv's hard face, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Jomon felt scared, more by the hardness than the ride itself, and realised that shouting and refusals were pushing Dhruv further away.

qa.q: Which of Jomon's changes led Dhruv to choose safely?
qa.a: Giving the real reason, the unlit highway stretch, and offering two safe options, so Dhruv could choose within limits.

qa.q: How did Dhruv's behaviour change after being given reasons and choices?
qa.a: Dhruv went from slamming doors and switching off his phone to picking the weekend option, asking for the lights to be checked and texting on arrival.

grounding: Shows a parent seeing that repeated refusals produced defiance and secrecy, and switching to reasons, choices within limits and connection.

passage:
Tuesday night
Divyansh locked his door again tonight. Third time this week. Since I banned phones at dinner and took away his cricket money for bad marks, he hardly speaks to me. Today I found out he failed a chemistry test and hid the paper; his tuition teacher told me, not him. My first thought: more rules. Then I remembered being fifteen, and Amma reading my diary. I didn't tell her anything for years after that.
So tonight I knocked and didn't lecture. I said the phone rule stays, but he can pick which meal it applies to, and the cricket money comes back if he shows me his plan for chemistry, not his marks. He opened the door halfway. We talked about the test. He's scared of it.
Nandini

qa.a: His tuition teacher told Nandini.

In their small town near Nashik, Manoj had made rule after rule for his son Kunal: no phone after seven, no friends' houses, no bike past the market. For a while it seemed to work.

Then the shopkeeper mentioned seeing Kunal at the highway petrol pump at night. Manoj found a second phone in Kunal's school bag.

He wanted to shout. Instead he sat on the charpai outside, breathing slowly. When Kunal came out, Manoj said, "I'm scared about the highway. That's why I made rules. But the rules just made you hide."

Kunal stared at his feet.

"Let's make them together," Manoj said. "Market and school roads okay. Tell me where you go. Highway only with me." Kunal nodded, and for the first time in weeks, sat down beside him.

qa.q: What did Manoj find in Kunal's school bag?
qa.a: He found a second phone in Kunal's school bag.

qa.q: How was Manoj feeling when he sat on the charpai breathing slowly?
qa.a: He felt angry and shaken, but also scared for Kunal and determined not to make things worse.

qa.q: What did Manoj do well when he talked to Kunal?
qa.a: He explained his fear, admitted the rules made Kunal hide, and made new limits together with him.

qa.q: How might Kunal feel sitting beside his father again?
qa.a: Kunal may feel relieved and a little ashamed, but also more respected and willing to be honest.

grounding: A parent sees strict rules produce secrecy and shifts to explaining reasons, offering choices within limits and staying connected.

passage:
In Lyon, Tariq had banned his daughter Noa from the skate park after she came home with a scraped knee. Then he banned the friends who went there. Then her phone at night.

By spring she'd stopped speaking at dinner. One Saturday Tariq found her skateboard hidden under the stairs, wheels still dusty.

He wanted to take it away. Instead he knocked on her door. "I'm frightened you'll get badly hurt. I went about it the wrong way."

Noa looked up, surprised.

"Helmet and pads, and you tell me when you go," he said. "And maybe show me a trick sometime."

The next week she texted him from the park, "Here. Helmet on." He smiled at his phone for a long time.

qa.q: What did Tariq find under the stairs?
qa.a: He found her skateboard hidden under the stairs.

qa.q: Why did Tariq choose to knock on Noa's door instead of taking the skateboard?
qa.a: He felt frightened for her but also saw that more bans were only pushing her away, so he wanted to reconnect.

qa.q: Which change helped, and why?
qa.a: Explaining his fear and setting a clear limit, helmet, pads and a message, gave Noa freedom she could accept.

qa.q: How might Noa see her father's new approach?
qa.a: Noa probably feels respected and less trapped, which is why she chose to text him from the park.

grounding: A father sees his strict rules produce secrecy, then explains his reasons and offers limited choices, staying connected.

At the parent-teacher meeting, Irfan sat across from Devika's class teacher and heard something he hadn't expected. "She's been skipping Friday tuition. She says she's at the library, but she's in the park with friends."
Irfan felt his face go hot. At home he had rules for everything: phone locked at eight, no outings on weekdays, no friends' houses. He had thought strictness kept her safe.
On the drive home, Devika stared out of the window, waiting for the shouting.
He didn't shout. "I'm not angry. I'm worried. My rules made you hide things, didn't they?"
A long pause. "You never say why," she said. "Just no."
That night he sat with her and they made a new list together: why each rule mattered, which ones could bend, and a Friday park hour if she texted him where she was. Devika added one line herself: I'll tell you the truth.

qa.a: Irfan felt embarrassed and worried, realising his strict rules had pushed Devika into hiding things.

qa.q: What new approach did Irfan take, and why is it wiser?
qa.a: Explaining the reasons for each rule, letting some bend and offering a Friday park hour with a text, which keeps limits and connection.

qa.a: Devika felt controlled without explanation, so hiding seemed easier than asking; reasons make cooperating easier.

grounding: Shows a father who sees his strict rules produce secrecy and shifts to reasons, choices within limits and connection.

passage:
Arnab,
I'm writing this because when we talk, we both end up shouting.
For a year I've made the rules: no gaming on weekdays, phone in my room at nine, no sleepovers. Every rule, I made alone. And every month you've found a way round one. The second phone. The late-night gaming at your friend's house. I've been angry. But lately I've been watching, and I think my rules are teaching you to hide, not to choose.
So I want to try something different. Here are my worries: your sleep, your eyes, your marks slipping. Now you tell me yours. Let's make three rules together, with choices inside them. Maybe gaming on Fridays and Saturdays, you pick the hours. And if something goes wrong, I want you to tell me, not hide it.
I'll be in the kitchen at seven on Sunday with chai.
Baba (Harsha)

qa.a: Harsha will be in the kitchen at seven on Sunday with chai.

qa.a: Sharing Harsha's worries, hearing Arnab's, and making three rules together with choices inside, so Arnab has less reason to rebel.

passage:
Asif, thanks for having me. I'm Jatin, and I came on your podcast to talk about the year I got parenting wrong.
My son turned fourteen, and I panicked. New rules every week. No friends after six. I checked his phone every night. When he wanted to try out for the football team, I said no, studies first.
And he changed. He got quiet. He deleted chats before I checked. Once I found out he'd been going to football practice for a month, telling me it was a science club.
The strictest months were the months he told me the least.
So I tried something my wife suggested. I stopped announcing rules and started explaining them. I said, "I worry about your marks. Here's why. What would you suggest?" He suggested football three days a week and study hours on the others. We shook on it.
He talks to me again. Not everything. But much more.

qa.q: What did Jatin's son say football practice was?
qa.a: He said it was a science club.

qa.q: What did Jatin feel when he found out about the month of football practice?
qa.a: Jatin felt shocked and hurt, and began to see that his strict rules were making his son hide things.

qa.q: What change did Jatin make, and why did it help?
qa.a: Jatin explained the reasons for his worries and asked his son for suggestions, which led to a fair deal of football three days a week.

qa.q: What were the strict months like for Jatin's son?
qa.a: The son felt controlled and went quiet, deleting chats and hiding football to protect his freedom.

grounding: Shows a father who saw strict rules produce secrecy and defiance and shifted to explaining reasons and agreeing choices within limits.

passage:
I'm Yusuf, and for most of last year my rules for Imran were simple: phone handed in at nine, no friends' houses, home straight after school. I said them loudly and often.
What I saw was a boy who went quiet. Single-word answers. A shut door. Then his sister told me he'd been using an old phone under his pillow, and that when he said he was at maths club, he was at the football ground. When I confronted him, he shouted, "You don't trust me about anything!" and slammed the door.
I sat on the stairs a long time. Rules I'd meant as protection were teaching him to hide.
So I changed. I told him why nine o'clock mattered to me: his sleep, his exams. I let him choose two evenings a week at the ground. I started walking him to practice.
Last Friday he texted: "Staying till 7, Abbu, okay?" He asked. That was new.

qa.q: Where was Imran when he said he was at maths club?
qa.a: He was at the football ground.

qa.q: What was Yusuf feeling as he sat on the stairs after the door slammed?
qa.a: Yusuf felt hurt and shaken, seeing that rules meant as protection were teaching Imran to hide.

qa.q: Which change made the biggest difference, and why?
qa.a: Explaining the reason for nine o'clock and giving choices within limits, because Imran no longer needed secrecy to feel some freedom.

qa.q: How did the strict rules feel to Imran?
qa.a: They felt like distrust about everything, which is why he hid a phone, lied about maths club and slammed the door.

grounding: Shows a parent seeing strict rules produce secrecy and defiance, then shifting to reasons, choices within limits and staying connected.
